hints: Think about which functional group containing nitrogen and oxygen can gain hydrogen to become $\text{NH}_2$ attached directly to a benzene ring.
Recall the classic metal plus concentrated acid combination used specifically for nitroarenes, and the heating needed for this reduction.
walkthrough:
Spot the change from starting material to product**
You are finishing with $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$. The benzene ring is already there, so the precursor must be a benzene ring carrying a nitrogen group that can be reduced. That classic precursor is the nitro group, $\text{NO}_2$, so start from nitrobenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2$.

Choose the reducing system for a nitroarene**
Reduction of $\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{NH}_2$ needs a powerful source of hydrogen. For aromatic nitro compounds the standard laboratory method is tin metal in concentrated hydrochloric acid: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2 + 6[H] \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ where $[H]$ is provided by $\text{Sn}$ + $\text{HCl}$.

Add the correct conditions**
This reduction is slow in the cold, so you heat the mixture, usually boiling under reflux, with concentrated $\text{HCl}$ to keep the reducing environment strongly acidic.

Final answer: organic compound: nitrobenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2$
reagents: $\text{Sn}$ and $\text{HCl}$
conditions: concentrated $\text{HCl}$ and heat / boil / reflux

hints: Count the carbons in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ and think which functional groups with the same carbon skeleton can be reduced to a primary amine.
Recall the single powerful hydride reagent that reduces both nitriles and amides to amines, which is different from the $\text{Sn}$/$\text{HCl}$ used for nitroarenes.
walkthrough:
Work backwards from propylamine**
Your target is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, a three carbon primary amine. Two functional groups reduce cleanly to this: a three carbon nitrile, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CN}$, or a three carbon amide, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2$. Both already contain the $\text{C}_3$ skeleton and nitrogen.

Select the hydride donor**
Nitriles and amides are reduced by lithium aluminium hydride: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CN} + 4[H] \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$$ $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2 + 4[H] \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ $\text{LiAlH}_4$ supplies hydride, $\text{H}^-$, and must be used in dry ether followed by acid work up. It is much stronger than $\text{NaBH}_4$, which cannot do this reduction.

Final answer: organic compound: propanenitrile, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CN}$ OR propanamide, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2$
reagent: $\text{LiAlH}_4$

hints: Think about how the $\text{NH}_2$ group activates a benzene ring very strongly, and which familiar orange reagent is decolourised with a white solid in that test.
Consider why phenylamine reacts without a catalyst or $\text{FeBr}_3$ while aliphatic amines like propylamine do not give this ring substitution product.
walkthrough:
Use the activation difference**
Picture the two amines. In propylamine the $\text{NH}_2$ is on an alkyl chain, no ring to substitute. In phenylamine the $\text{NH}_2$ lone pair is delocalised into the ring, making the ring extremely activated toward electrophiles. Bromine water is the perfect probe for this.

Describe the observed test**
Add aqueous bromine, $\text{Br}_2(aq)$, to each amine. With phenylamine the orange solution is decolourised and a white precipitate appears immediately: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + 3\text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_2\text{Br}_3\text{NH}_2 + 3\text{HBr}$$ Propylamine gives no such precipitate under these conditions.

Draw the precipitated product**
Because activation is so strong, substitution happens three times, at both ortho positions and the para position. Draw a benzene ring with $\text{NH}_2$ at the top, $\text{Br}$ on the two carbons next to it (positions 2 and 6) and $\text{Br}$ opposite it (position 4). That is 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine.

Final answer: testing reagent: bromine (aq)
amine that gives a precipitate: phenylamine, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$
structure of precipitate: 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine, benzene ring with $\text{NH}_2$ at position 1 and $\text{Br}$ at positions 2, 4 and 6

hints: Start by writing the order you expect from weakest to strongest base, remembering that aromatic amines are famously weaker than ammonia while aliphatic amines are stronger.
Recall the Bronsted-Lowry definition of a base in terms of what the nitrogen lone pair must do to a proton, $\text{H}^+$.
Compare what happens to the nitrogen lone pair in phenylamine, where it can overlap with the benzene $\pi$ system, versus in ammonia where it is localised.
Consider how the propyl alkyl group pushes electron density toward nitrogen compared with just hydrogen atoms in ammonia.
walkthrough:
State the basicity order**
Basic strength is: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 < \text{NH}_3 < \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$$ Phenylamine is least basic, propylamine is most basic, ammonia is in the middle.

Link basicity to the lone pair**
Think like a proton, $\text{H}^+$. A Bronsted-Lowry base must donate a lone pair to accept $\text{H}^+$. The easier that lone pair is to share, the stronger the base. All three have one lone pair on nitrogen, so the difference is how available that pair is.

Explain why phenylamine is weakest**
In $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ the nitrogen p orbital overlaps with the benzene $\pi$ system. The lone pair is delocalised into the ring. Because it is partly pulled away from nitrogen, it is much less ready to bond to $\text{H}^+$. The resulting phenylammonium ion is also less stabilised because delocalisation is lost on protonation.

Explain why propylamine is strongest**
In $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ there is no ring to drain the lone pair. Instead the propyl alkyl group is electron donating by the inductive effect. It pushes electron density onto nitrogen, increasing the negative character and making the lone pair more easily donated to $\text{H}^+$ than the lone pair in $\text{NH}_3$, where only hydrogen atoms are attached.

Final answer: phenylamine < ammonia < propylamine (least basic to most basic)
A base uses a nitrogen lone pair to accept a proton, $\text{H}^+$.
In phenylamine the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring $\pi$ system, so it is less available to accept $\text{H}^+$.
In propylamine the alkyl group is electron donating, increasing electron density on nitrogen, so the lone pair is more available than in $\text{NH}_3$.
